desc:
In one operation you may choose any node of a binary tree and increase its value by 1. Values are never decreased. Find the minimum number of operations needed so that all root-to-leaf paths have the same sum (a leaf is a node with no children; the sum of a path is the sum of the values of its nodes).

A tree with at most one leaf already satisfies the condition, so the answer is 0 for it, including the empty tree.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3] the two path sums are 3 and 4, so one operation (raise the left leaf, node 2, by 1) is enough and the answer is 1. For tree = [1, 5, 2, 2, 3, 3, 1] the answer is 6.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Raising a node raises every path that goes through it. Where is it cheapest to fix a difference between two sibling subtrees?
At a node whose two child subtrees have different best path sums, the weaker side has to catch up. Increasing the child on the weaker side lifts all its paths at once.

Compute f[v], the largest sum of a downward path starting at v. Each node with two children contributes |f[left] - f[right]| to the answer; nodes with one child or none contribute nothing. Sum these up.
editorial: Only the relative sums inside each subtree matter at a node: raising a node shifts all leaf sums below it by the same amount, so it cannot reduce a difference between the two sides of any node underneath it. Differences can only be closed by raising nodes inside the weaker child's subtree.

Process bottom-up. Suppose every subtree below v is already balanced (all its downward paths have equal sum), with common sum f[child]. If v has two children with f[left] != f[right], the cheapest fix is to add the difference to the weaker child itself, which raises all of its paths with a single increment amount of |f[left] - f[right]|. No cheaper repair exists because the paths through the weaker side must gain at least that much while the operations inside the other subtree cannot help. After this, both sides have equal sums and f[v] = val[v] + max(f[left], f[right]).

So the answer is the sum of |f[left] - f[right]| over the nodes with two children. A node with one child needs nothing. A single backwards pass over the level-order array gives O(n) time and O(n) space. The statement keeps values at most 100 so that the result fits in 32 bits.
